name: Silicone scar tape
lead: Silicone scar tape, also called silicone gel sheeting, is a thin, adhesive silicone sheet worn over a healing or healed scar. It is used mainly for raised hypertrophic and keloid scars and is sold over the counter for surgical and other scars. Treatment typically involves wearing the sheet for many hours a day over a period of months.

Wikipedia describes silicone treatments as commonly used to prevent scarring and to improve the look of existing scars, while noting that a Cochrane meta-analysis found weak evidence that gel sheeting helps prevent scarring and that the studies were of poor quality and susceptible to bias [1][3]. The site rates the evidence moderate and the outcome durable, with the one-line description that it flattens some raised scars over months of wear. The sheets are not described as removing a mature, flat scar.

paras: A scar is an area of fibrous tissue that replaces normal skin after injury. Scar collagen is arranged differently from that in normal skin, with cross-linked, aligned fibres, and skin scars lack sweat glands and hair follicles [1]. Hypertrophic scars are raised above the surrounding skin, typically appear within about 4 to 8 weeks after wound closure and stay within the wound boundary, whereas keloids can extend beyond the original wound and are more common in people with darker skin. Atrophic scars are sunken, often after acne [1]. Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, says most scars fade over up to two years or more but cannot be completely removed, and that early redness fades as the scar matures [2].

The sheets are flexible silicone, usually self-adhesive and often reusable after washing. They are applied over closed skin, not open wounds. In the Wikipedia overview of scar treatment, silicone sheeting appears in the dressings and topical silicone category alongside pressure dressings, which are common in burn and hypertrophic scar management though supporting evidence is described as lacking [1]. Other approaches listed there include chemical peels, fillers, lasers, steroid injections, surgical revision, massage and radiotherapy, each with varying evidence [1].

The mechanism is not settled. Proposed explanations include hydration and occlusion of the stratum corneum, which is thought to reduce fibroblast activity and collagen overproduction, and effects of mild pressure or temperature under the sheet. Wikipedia notes that mechanical stress on a wound can stimulate scarring and that reducing stress on wounds has been associated with smaller scars [1].

The principal evidence is a Cochrane systematic review, Silicone gel sheeting for preventing and treating hypertrophic and keloid scars, published in 2013 [3]. As summarised by Wikipedia, the review found weak evidence that silicone gel sheeting helps prevent scarring, and the studies it examined were of poor quality and susceptible to bias [1]. The site's research notes add that some data suggested possible benefit for people prone to abnormal scarring, while benefit for treatment could not be clearly confirmed.
A 2019 protocol published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews set out plans to review silicone gel sheeting for treating hypertrophic scars [4].

Wikipedia also reports a study from the Catholic University of Korea concluding that verapamil-releasing silicone gel reduced scar height and redness in a hypertrophic scar model compared with conventional silicone gel [1]. This concerns a different, experimental product.

A 2024 laboratory study incorporated antimicrobial ceragenins into silicone- and polyacrylate-based medical adhesives and scar tape adhesives to reduce microbial colonisation, finding reduced microbial growth over weeks and no dermal irritation in an in vivo model [5]. This was a materials study and did not evaluate scar appearance.

Side effects described for silicone sheeting are mainly itching, rash and skin maceration under the sheet; it is not intended for use over open wounds. The 2013 Cochrane review's overall judgement of poor trial quality means improvement estimates are uncertain [1][3]. Wikipedia lists other treatments with their own risks, such as filler reactions and the cautions needed for peels in darker skin and keloid-prone people [1].

Silicone scar sheets are listed in the body-care shelf as a low-cost option for raised scars, including acne and surgical scars. Forum threads retrieved for this entry did not address silicone sheeting; scars appeared only in unrelated contexts, so no community-specific protocol or claims could be documented.
